name: Hana Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the line lead on filling line two at Greenvale Dairy. We fill and seal yoghurt pots, about twenty thousand an hour when it's behaving, then they go through the case packer and onto the new palletising robot at the end. My day is changeovers, from strawberry to plain, say, with a full clean in between, plus chasing faults and keeping four operators and a trainee moving. I've been at Greenvale eleven years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love fault-finding. When the sealer starts leaving wrinkles I want to know why before the engineer even gets there. What drains me is the paperwork, honestly, or it used to. Now I talk my shift report into an AI app on the drive home and it turns it into something tidy, and I use it to dig through the fault logs too. My partner Jonas teases me that I talk to my phone more than to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? I'd be a little disappointed, to be honest. I've had fun with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, and anyone who isn't using it for the boring bits is missing out. At work I'd keep showing people how I do my reports. Online I'd say the hype was silly, but the tool's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be fine for me. I'm good at my job, the line still needs people, and the factory isn't going anywhere. If anything I'd be a bit bored, because I like it when things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd keep using AI for reports and fault logs, and I'd ask Greenvale to let me run a short session for the other line leads on how I use it. We'd keep our three months of savings and maybe finally do the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe slightly flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be bored. Is that a real feeling for you at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is. The best year I had was when they put the palletiser in, because I volunteered to be the person who learned it first. I was the one the engineer phoned at midnight. I'd miss that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your line would be glad to hear AI was mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernadette, who's been packing for twenty-two years and still calls the palletiser 'that thing'. She'd be relieved. She'd bring in a cake, probably.

S0.say: She'd say it's still a good tool for the boring bits and keep showing colleagues how she writes reports with it, while saying online that the hype was silly but the tool is real.
S0.think: It would be fine for her, since her job and the factory are secure, but she'd be a bit bored because she enjoys change.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for reports and fault logs and offers to run a short session for the other line leads. Keeps three months of savings and maybe does the bathroom.
S0.quote: I was the one the engineer phoned at midnight.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is the rare operator who would be mildly disappointed by a quiet future. Her proudest work moment is being first to learn the palletiser. She already teaches others, and her instinct is to share what she knows rather than guard it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I think is the real one. And I'd want to be at the front of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to come with training for everyone, not just the keen ones like me, and the union should make that part of every deal. I'd say it at work and I'd be the person posting the training links in the group chat. Change can be good, but only if people aren't left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. Somebody has to run and fix the robots, and I'd go for that job. But I can see half my line not making the jump, and I'd feel guilty being the one who did fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Greenvale to put me through an automation technician apprenticeship, the two-year evening one at the college, and if they wouldn't pay I'd look at paying part of it myself. I'd keep using AI to learn the control systems. I'd push the union rep to get training written into the next agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a knot of guilt underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really pay for the course yourself, with three months saved and a mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of it, yes. It's about the cost of a cheap holiday per term. Jonas and I talked about something like it last year, and he said go for it, as long as I'm not out four nights a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernadette, definitely. And Kofi, who's thirty and quick but can barely read English, so the online courses are no good for him. I'd want the company to do training in the room, with a person, for people like Kofi.

S1.say: She'd say change must come with training for everyone, written into union deals, and she'd be the one posting training links in the group chat.
S1.think: She sees it as good for her, since someone must run and fix the robots, but she feels guilty knowing half her line may not make the jump.
S1.do: Asks Greenvale to fund a two-year evening automation technician apprenticeship and would pay part herself if needed. Uses AI to learn the control systems and pushes the union to write training into the next agreement.
S1.quote: I'd want the company to do training in the room, with a person, for people like Kofi.
S1.fieldNote: Hana moves first and is ready to spend her own money on it, after talking it through with Jonas. Her progressive outlook shows up as worry for colleagues who can't take the same path, like Kofi with his limited reading. She feels guilt about doing well, which she says openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one's different. If the robot can fix the robot, my plan doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to cope with alone, so the government needs to step in with real money, wage support and help with housing costs. I'd say the companies getting rich from it should pay for that. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd still get a year or two more than most, because someone has to help move the line over, and I'd make sure that person was me. But after that, I don't know. Two years isn't long enough to become anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to my manager and say, put me on the changeover team. I'd use every evening to learn how these new systems are set up, with AI as my teacher. At home we'd stop spending on anything extra and push the savings towards six months. I'd join whatever campaign the union started for wage support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops. But I'd be busy, and being busy helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ivy and Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ivy's eleven and she reads the news on her tablet, so she'd already know. I'd tell her the truth: Mum's job might change, and we've got a plan. Leo's eight, I'd just tell him nothing's changing at home, because for him it wouldn't, not right away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With just two years, does being quick to adapt still help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It buys me months, not years. Being adaptable is great when there's somewhere to adapt to. In two years there might not be anywhere left to land.

S2.say: She'd say it's too fast to cope with alone and the government must step in with wage support and help with housing costs, paid for by the companies getting rich from it.
S2.think: She expects a year or two more than most by getting onto the team that moves the line over, but after that she doesn't know, and two years isn't long enough to become something new.
S2.do: Asks her manager to put her on the changeover team and spends evenings learning the new systems with AI. Stops extra spending, pushes savings towards six months and joins a union wage-support campaign.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a dropping stomach, but helped by staying busy.
S2.quote: Being adaptable is great when there's somewhere to adapt to.
S2.fieldNote: The fast AGI picture breaks Hana's plan from the steady one, because her robot-technician route disappears if robots fix themselves. She still acts first and puts herself on the changeover team, but she knows it only buys months. She'd tell her older child the truth and shield the younger one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough for me to do something useful with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance if we use it, so get the training going now and get a support system ready before 2031. I'd say it at work, I'd say it to the council, and I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right for most of those five years. I'd do the automation course and get into the commissioning side, setting up the new kit. By the end I might be out of work like everyone else, but I'd have had time to pay down the mortgage and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the evening automation course and offer to be the plant's go-to person for every new system. I'd put aside a bit more each month to get to six months. Jonas and I would talk seriously about whether he keeps teaching, because schools might hold on longer than factories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be out of work at the end anyway. Why put in the effort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the effort pays for five years of good wages and keeps me in the room where decisions get made. And I'd rather be the one helping Bernadette and Kofi through it than standing next to them not knowing anything. Also, honestly, I'd enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between two years and five, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm scrambling. Five, I can do one proper course and get a couple of years' value out of it. That's the difference between surviving and making something of it.

S3.say: She'd say five years is a real chance if training starts now and a support system is ready before 2031, and she'd raise it at work, with the council and through petitions.
S3.think: She expects to be fine for most of the five years by moving into commissioning new kit, and even if she loses work at the end, she'd have paid down the mortgage and saved.
S3.do: Starts the evening automation course in the first year and makes herself the plant's go-to person for new systems. Saves towards six months and talks with Jonas about whether his teaching job is the steadier one.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.
S3.quote: Two years, I'm scrambling. Five, I can do one proper course and get a couple of years' value out of it.
S3.fieldNote: Hana weighs the five-year picture practically: one course, a couple of years of value from it, a mortgage pushed down. She accepts she may still end up out of work and does the work anyway, partly to help colleagues and partly because she enjoys it. She openly considers the family leaning on Jonas's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in my world. Ten years ago we didn't have a single robot on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to build something fair: shorter weeks, public retraining, and the gains shared out. I'd want my union and my party talking about it now, not in 2035. And I'd say to people at work, start learning, it's not as scary when you get your hands on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for most of it. I'd move into automation, then maybe into training other people, which I'm good at. By the time it all arrives, I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and the house would be mostly paid. The big question is whether the gains get shared or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the automation apprenticeship over two years without killing myself, then look for a trainer role in the industry. I'd keep the savings steady and overpay the mortgage a little. I'd get involved with the union's education committee, which I've always meant to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end point, but honestly a bit hopeful about the journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the big question is whether the gains get shared. What would that look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people who taught the machines get something for it. A shorter week on the same pay, or a share in the company, or a proper public income. If it's all just profit for whoever owns the robots, then ten years just means a slower way to the same unfairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you change anything for Ivy and Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd steer them towards things with people in them, teaching, caring, building communities. And I'd teach them to use the tools from now. Ivy's already asking me how my app writes the reports.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is time to build something fair, with shorter weeks, public retraining and shared gains, and she'd urge colleagues to start learning because it's less scary hands-on.
S4.think: She expects to do well for most of the decade, moving into automation and then training, and to reach the end with the kids grown and the house mostly paid. Her big question is whether the gains are shared.
S4.do: Does the automation apprenticeship over two years, then looks for a trainer role in the industry. Keeps savings steady, overpays the mortgage a little and joins the union's education committee.
S4.feel: Uneasy about the end point but a bit hopeful about the road there.
S4.quote: Ten years ago we didn't have a single robot on the line.
S4.fieldNote: Hana measures ten years against her own memory of the line before the palletiser. Her worry has moved almost entirely from her own job to fairness: whether the people who taught the machines get anything back. She'd steer her children towards work with people in it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Being good at change doesn't help if the change is a cliff. What would help is a wage guarantee for people moved off the line, paid by the companies that put in the machines, and free evening courses that people like Kofi can actually follow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want the robots if everyone was looked after. And the answer is yes, honestly. Washing down a filling line at three in the morning isn't some precious tradition. I just don't want the people who did it for twenty years to get nothing.

headlineQuote: Washing down a filling line at three in the morning isn't some precious tradition.
portrait: Hana Abbott is 43 and leads filling line two at Greenvale Dairy, where she volunteered to be first to learn the palletising robot and now uses AI daily for reports and fault logs. She sees the steady change picture as a chance and would pay part of an automation course herself. Fast AGI breaks her plan, because robots fixing robots leaves nowhere to adapt to, and she becomes anxious, though she'd still put herself on the changeover team. With five or ten years she grows hopeful about the road but keeps asking whether the gains will be shared with the people who taught the machines. Her worry is mostly for colleagues like Bernadette and Kofi.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because being good at change doesn't help when the change is a cliff.
whatWouldHelp: A wage guarantee for workers moved off the line, paid by the companies bringing in machines, and free evening courses that people with limited reading can follow.
